title: 26. Externally validated bioelectrical impedance–based screening model for caseous lymphadenitis in goats.
content:
Abstract
Caseous lymphadenitis (CL), caused by Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis, is a chronic and economically significant disease affecting goat production. Early detection is essential to limit transmission; however, field-deployable screening tools remain scarce. This study evaluated multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) as a non-invasive screening method using externally validated statistical models. Impedance-derived frequency features were analyzed via logistic regression and assessed with Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) validation to determine animal-level generalizability. The overall discrimination achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.60 (95% CI: 0.48–0.72). LOSO validation revealed inter-animal variability (mean AUC 0.43 ± 0.12; range 0.30–0.60), reflecting biological heterogeneity in disease expression. Incorporating nonlinear spectral effects into baseline linear frequency models improved classification performance (ΔAUC = 0.05). Reclassification analysis demonstrated Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI = 0.18; 95% CI: 0.04–0.31) and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI = 0.04; 95% CI: 0.01–0.08), confirming enhanced identification of CL-positive cases. Calibration analysis indicated moderate agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, with underestimation in lower-risk categories (0.20–0.30). Decision curve analysis showed a positive net benefit across threshold probabilities from 0.05 to 0.75, peaking near a 0.15 threshold (∼0.35), supporting its use as a herd-level screening tool prioritizing sensitivity. Mahalanobis distance analysis confirmed multivariate spectral separation (median CL: 2.3 versus healthy: 1.5), indicating biologically measurable electrical differences. These findings demonstrate that multi-frequency impedance captures clinically relevant electrical alterations associated with CL. Although discrimination remains moderate, external validation, reclassification metrics, and decision analysis support the method’s translational potential for integration into routine herd health monitoring programs.
